# How to Automatically Sort Your Emails with AI (No Coding Needed)

> **In short:** Gmail's built-in AI already splits your inbox into tabs like Primary, Promotions and Updates. To sort by *meaning* — invoices in one folder, family messages in another — you describe what you want in plain English to a chatbot, paste the result into Gmail's filter creator, and the rule runs on every new email from then on.

You're two coffees deep and you've just spent 40 minutes clearing yesterday's inbox. Three emails you actually needed are buried under newsletters, shopping receipts and a Slack thread that should've stayed in Slack. Sound familiar?

Here's the thing: AI can do the triaging for you. Not with code, but with a sentence you'd write to a helpful colleague. In the next few minutes, you'll set up rules that move emails automatically — based on what they mean, not just who sent them.

## What you need before you start

- A **Gmail** account (a free personal one works — the steps below don't require Google Workspace or a paid plan).
- A **web browser** on a laptop or desktop. The mobile Gmail app has fewer options for creating filters, so use a browser.
- Access to a **chatbot** like ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Any of them will do, including the free tiers. You'll use it once or twice per filter.
- About **15 minutes** for the first filter. Adding more filters afterwards takes 1–2 minutes each.

> 💬 **Quick jargon check:** A "filter" in Gmail is just an automatic rule — *if a new email matches these words, do this with it*. A "label" is like a folder, except one email can sit under several labels at once.

## Step 1 — Turn on Gmail's built-in AI categories

Gmail already uses AI (a machine-learning model running on Google's servers) to sort incoming mail into coloured tabs. If you've never touched this, they're probably switched off.

1. Open Gmail in your browser and click the **gear icon** (⚙️) in the top-right corner.
2. Click **"See all settings"** in the menu that appears.
3. Click the **"Inbox"** tab along the top of the settings page.
4. Scroll down to **"Categories"**. Tick the boxes for **Primary, Promotions, Social, Updates** and **Forums**.
5. At the top, make sure the **"Inbox type"** dropdown is set to a view that supports categories — **"Default"** works. If the tabs don't show after saving, try a different option here.
6. Scroll to the bottom and click **"Save Changes"**.

💬 **Example prompt to try later:** *"Catch any email from my child's school in one label."*

**You'll know it worked when** you refresh your inbox and see coloured tabs (Primary, Promotions, etc.) along the top, and existing newsletters have already moved into Promotions without you doing anything.

## Step 2 — Create the labels you want emails sorted into

Gmail calls folders **labels**. You'll need to make these before filters can move messages into them.

1. Look at the **left-hand sidebar**. Scroll down past Inbox, Sent and Drafts until you see your existing labels.
2. Click **"Create new label"**. (If it's hidden, click **"More"** at the bottom of the label list first.)
3. Type a short name like **Finances**, **Family**, **Work-Urgent** or **Receipts**.
4. Optional: tick **"Nest label under"** to put it inside another label — e.g. **Receipts** living under **Finances**.
5. Click **"Create"**.

Repeat for each folder. A starter set:
- **Work/Urgent** — clients, deadlines, your manager
- **Finances** — banks, invoices, receipts
- **Family** — partner, kids' school, relatives
- **Newsletters** — things you read but don't act on

💬 **Example prompt to use later:** *"Give me a Gmail search query that catches invoices or statements from any Australian bank or telco."*

**You'll know it worked when** the new labels appear in the left sidebar. If one doesn't, refresh the page.

## Step 3 — Ask a chatbot to write the Gmail search query

This is the bit that makes it "AI" without any code. Instead of guessing Gmail's search syntax, you describe what you want in plain English and let the chatbot translate.

1. Open a chatbot in another browser tab — ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type a prompt that says what you want caught. Be specific about the kind of email, not just keywords. For example:

   💬 *"Give me a Gmail search query using OR, from:, subject: and has: operators that catches invoices or receipts from Australian banks and telcos like CommBank, NAB, Telstra and Optus. I want it to match the word 'invoice', 'statement', 'receipt' or 'payment' anywhere in the email."*

3. Copy the search query the chatbot gives you. It'll look something like:
   `(from:commbank.com.au OR from:nab.com.au OR from:telstra.com.au) AND (invoice OR statement OR receipt OR payment)`

You don't need to memorise Gmail's syntax — that's the chatbot's job. If the query looks wrong, just tell the chatbot what to fix: *"Make it match 'invoice' anywhere in the email, not just the subject."*

**You'll know it worked when** you have a one-line query containing words like OR, AND or parentheses. Skip this step if you only need a simple "from this sender" rule — you can type those yourself in the next step.

## Step 4 — Build the filter in Gmail using the chatbot's query

Now you paste the chatbot's query into Gmail's filter tool and tell Gmail what to do with matching emails.

1. Click the **gear icon** (⚙️) → **"See all settings"** → **"Filters and Blocked Addresses"** tab.
2. Click **"Create a new filter"** (a blue link/button — Gmail has moved it around over the years, but the words are the same).
3. Leave most fields blank. Click into the **"Has the words"** box and paste the chatbot's query.
4. Click **"Search"** at the bottom-right. **Do this before anything else.** It shows how many existing emails match — if it's zero, the query's broken.
5. If the count looks right, click **"Create filter"** at the bottom-right to continue.
6. On the next screen, tick the actions you want:
   - **Skip the Inbox (Archive it)** — keep this *off* at first
   - **Apply the label:** — choose your label from Step 2 (e.g. **Finances**)
   - **Mark as read** — optional, useful for newsletters
   - **Also apply filter to matching conversations** — only if you want old emails moved too
7. Click **"Create filter"** again to save.

💬 **Example action combo:** *Skip the Inbox* + *Apply label: Finances*. Invoices will silently land in your Finances label and never appear in the main inbox.

**You'll know it worked when** you send yourself a test email (from a second Gmail address, with "invoice" in the subject) and it lands in the right label within a minute.

## Step 5 — Refine the rule and add more over time

The first filter rarely nails it on the first go. That's normal — refinement is part of the process.

1. Over the next few days, peek at the label a few times. Are emails landing there that shouldn't? Or are you missing things you wanted caught?
2. If something's off, paste the chatbot's query back into the chatbot and describe the problem. For example:

   💬 *"This Gmail query is too broad — it's matching every email from anyone with 'comm' in their address. Tighten it to only emails from commbank.com.au, nab.com.au, westpac.com.au and anz.com.au, and require the word 'statement' OR 'invoice' to appear in the subject line."*

3. To edit an existing filter: **Settings → Filters and Blocked Addresses** → find the rule → click **"edit"** on the right → change the search text → save.
4. To add another rule, repeat Steps 3 and 4 with a new prompt.

A rough rule: aim for **3–5 filters total** in your first week. More than that and you'll spend more time maintaining them than they save you.

**You'll know it worked when** your main inbox is mostly messages that actually need you, the busy stuff is already sorted into side labels, and your morning coffee stays warm.

## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1 — Skipping the "Search" preview before creating the filter.**
Gmail lets you click straight through to "Create filter" without checking how many existing emails match. If your query has a typo, you silently create a rule that catches nothing.
**Fix:** Always click **"Search"** in Step 4 *before* clicking "Create filter". Look at the count. If it's zero, or wildly off (say, 8,000 matches when you expected 20), fix the query with the chatbot first.

**Mistake 2 — Creating the filter before you make the label.**
If you tick "Apply the label: Receipts" but never made a label called Receipts, Gmail silently skips that action. The filter runs but nothing moves.
**Fix:** Always do Step 2 (create labels) before Step 4 (build filters). If you rename a label later, go back and edit any filters that used the old name — otherwise they break.

**Mistake 3 — "AND" appearing in the chatbot's query where you meant "OR".**
When you say "catch emails about invoices or receipts," the chatbot might return a query that requires *both* words. You'll catch almost nothing, because most invoices only say "invoice", not "invoice receipt".
**Fix:** In your prompt, spell it out: *"match if ANY of these words appear."* If the returned query uses AND where you meant OR, tell the chatbot: *"Change every AND in that query to OR."*

**Mistake 4 — Filtering out things you actually needed.**
"Skip the Inbox" removes a message from your main view entirely. If you accidentally catch the wrong thing, you might not see it for days.
**Fix:** For the first week of any new filter, leave **"Skip the Inbox"** *unticked*. Let matching emails stay in the inbox but get the label. Once you're confident the rule is catching only the right things, then go back and tick "Skip the Inbox".

## What this means for you

- **If you're managing a busy personal inbox:** Start with one filter for newsletters or shopping receipts — that's the highest-volume stuff and the easiest win. Add a second filter for bills and statements once the first one feels solid.
- **If you use email for work:** Set up a **Work/Urgent** label and ask the chatbot to catch emails from your manager, key clients or specific project keywords. Keep "Skip the Inbox" off for the first week so you can sanity-check what gets caught.
- **If you're new to AI tools:** This is a low-risk way to start. You're not handing the chatbot access to your inbox — you're just asking it to write a one-line search query. The chatbot never sees your actual messages.
